sequencing_rationale: Planning and source control come first because both projects that follow are graded on increments landed in version control, not on a single final commit; a learner who cannot branch and commit cannot show the work the later lessons ask for. Defect handling sits between the first and second project so the second project can be run as a report-fix-verify loop against real reported issues. The three projects grow in scope (single widget, data-driven page, portfolio piece) so the same skills are exercised at increasing independence, and the final one adds the demo because the catalog's presentation competency needs a real artifact to present. SCOPE ASSUMPTIONS: the intake description is truncated mid-word and names only "programming projects using JavaScript ... fundamentals of programming and web page construction", with three projects and 30 hours as the only firm evidence, so the outline assumes browser JavaScript against the DOM with no framework and no build tooling beyond a package manager. Assumed in scope: DOM work, fetching and rendering remote data, module organization, git workflow, debugging, and a presented portfolio piece. Assumed out of scope: React (react100 owns it), server-side JavaScript (node101 owns it), and automated test frameworks (node200 owns them). A reviewer who knows what the cut-off sentence said should correct the project briefs first.

proposed_competencies.competency_text: The learner can decompose a larger programming problem into functions and modules with single responsibilities.
proposed_competencies.rationale: Every project in this course is graded partly on decomposition, but the catalog's D2-S1 competencies stop at 'build program features' and never name breaking a problem down, which the truncated intake description appears to have been describing when it was cut off.

assets.description: A feature branch created from main, receiving three commits, then merging back through a reviewed pull request.
The states a reported defect moves through from report to verified closure, including the paths back when it cannot be reproduced and when a fix fails verification.
